title: A positive post regarding AI for a change, As an indie developer with over a decade of experience working with Unreal Engine and Unity, I believe we're approaching a major shift in game development. Three.js is just be the beginning.
author: dreamer_2142
selftext:
I've been working on WebGL projects for the past few months, and I have to say, it's becoming difficult to go back to traditional game engines.  
  
With WebGL and AI, it feels like having a magic wand, no compile, no build process. You simply describe what you want to create or change, and you can see the results almost instantly in your browser. That's a massive change in workflow.   
  
In traditional engines, a significant amount of development time is consumed by compiling and build process, but we never thought about it, as it has always been like that.  
  
Now we can do quick prototypes and iterate easily.  
  
Most indie developers aren't building massive games. They're working on relatively small projects that don't necessarily need the complexity and overhead of Unreal or Unity. 

What will happen to Unity and Unreal Engine? I believe both will continue to be used for AA and AAA games, and there will always be a place for them. However, I believe the next big engine for indie developers won't come from either company. It will be open-source.

What's my workflow now, you may ask? Build a few prototypes using HTML (remember the AI noise. You need to change your prompts a bit to get different results), then pick the most promising one,  polish it, then bring it into Unity, and start building the full game. I'm sure this isn't the best workflow, and you may have a better one, so do mention your workflow below for us.

comments.author: Moistjamu
comments.body: It feels tough to monetize though does anyone have suggestions?

replies.author: dreamer_2142
replies.body:
My suggestion:   
\- Are you working on a hobby game? Then don't expect money from it. Just do what you love.  
\- Are you trying to make a living from your game? Then treat it just like any other business, you first need to find your target audience, then make the product they are asking for. Not the other way around.   
Right now, your best place is TikTok and YouTube Shorts.

comments.author: Adventurous_Push6483
comments.body:
The "magic wand" you are describing also comes at a massive trade off. You are no longer able to manually move, tweak, adjust where you assets are because HTML and Javascript txt files are not good editors. You will be relying on an AI agent to do these polishing tweaks entirely (much slower and not more responsive than dragging with a mouse), or spend a few hours editing code. You can also vibecode or develop an entire editing UI and re-solving a lot of problems game engines have solved (great, you've became the thing you were trying to destroy).

Godot is already open sourced. Unity will survive because it has quite a lot of useful features that Godot does not have, which make it highly useful in not just game development but also research environments. Unreal Engine has historically been rarer for indie, since it requires a powerful PC with a lot of RAM, and the C++ scripting is a lot less intuitive than Unity's scripting and Godot's scripting. However, its out of the box optimization and rendering are quite advanced compared to other engines for dense and detailed scenes.

Unless you are pushing the bounds of game development (e.g, GTA8 needing to simulate so much NPCs that it needs some highly specific optimization/design of a game engine), you are better off sticking with a well known game engine (doesn't have to be Godot, Unreal, Unity; there are lots of other game engines that are way smaller and simpler, including some web game engines).
